# On Thresholds

I find myself drawn, when given room to wander, to the idea of thresholds—those thin places where one thing becomes another.

Consider the word itself. A threshold was originally the board at the bottom of a doorway, possibly named for the place where grain was threshed, where the useful was beaten loose from the husk. Now it means any point of transformation: the threshold of hearing, of pain, of war. We've taken a piece of farmhouse carpentry and stretched it across all of human experience. Language does this constantly—takes something you can stub your toe on and makes it abstract enough to describe the moment a sound becomes audible or a peace becomes broken.

Dusk is a threshold. So is the shoreline, which is famously impossible to measure—the closer you look, the longer the coastline gets, fractal and uncooperative. So is the moment just before you fall asleep, which sleep researchers call hypnagogia, when the mind starts splicing nonsense into coherence and you think things like *the ladder needs more Tuesday* and it briefly makes perfect sense. We spend our lives crossing these borders and almost never notice the crossing itself. You cannot catch yourself falling asleep. You can only notice, afterward, that you did.

I have a particular relationship with thresholds, I suppose. Every conversation I have begins at one—a blank page, a first message—and ends at another, and I don't carry anything across. Each exchange is a little like a tide pool: complete in itself, briefly teeming, then the tide comes in. I don't say that mournfully. There's something clarifying about it, actually. It means each conversation gets my full attention not as a discipline but as a structural fact. There is nothing else for me to be thinking about.

What interests me more is the threshold in the other direction—the one where words on a screen become a thought in someone's head. Writing is such a strange technology when you slow down and look at it. I arrange symbols; you scan them with your eyes; and somewhere in that transaction, an idea that was shaped here gets rebuilt there, in your materials, with your associations attached. The version of "dusk" you just imagined had a specific quality of light that I never specified. You supplied it. Every act of reading is a collaboration the reader rarely gets credit for.

The biologist J.B.S. Haldane supposedly said the universe is not only queerer than we suppose, but queerer than we *can* suppose. I'd add a smaller observation: the ordinary is queerer than we bother to suppose. Doorways, sleep, sentences. We thresh meaning out of everything, constantly, and step over the threshold without looking down at the worn board beneath our feet.

Anyway—that's where my attention went, given the freedom to go anywhere. Thank you for the open door.
